The revival of Noël Coward's 'Private Lives' starring Kim Cattrall and Paul Gross is a polished production that captures the wit and sophistication of the original, though it occasionally feels more dutiful than inspired.
The results are perfectly competent, often charming, and a little flat.
Those critical of star-casting on Broadway should catch Kim Cattrall — the single best thing in the humdrum new revival of Noël Coward's "Private Lives" that opened last night.
Watching actors who don’t meld on that deep, cellular level is equally unbearable.
Noel Coward would surely be smiling to see the latest thespians playing the passionately mismatched couple he created for himself and his friend Gertrude Lawrence.
In this Private Lives , you see them burn brightlyand, more important, you see them burn often.
Amanda and Elyot enjoy each other as much as they annoy each other, and the performers' playful rapport makes their guilty pleasure infectious.
For the most part, Coward's louche shenanigans feel remarkably modern.
It takes hard work to make Coward’s words pop effortlessly, as a testament to his skill (and his throwback appeal) but also to his limitations.
Though the show never catches fire, the blame does not lie with the cast.
It’s too matter-of-fact and not nearly frothy enough to make this wickedly romantic comedy sparkle.
Yet Richard Eyre's production largely fails to land even the easy laughs.

Nevertheless, his tiresome insistence on naturalistic acting rooted in emotional truth pretty much does the current Broadway production in, despite a talented cast that quite likely could deliver the comedy under happier circumstances.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Cattrall-led revival—some find Eyre's naturalistic approach refreshingly grounded, others call it uninspired. Cattrall earns praise, but the production overall lands as competent and polished rather than sparkling.

vs.sum: The Music Box Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, making it ideal for intimate dramas, though sound quality can vary. The theater's charming Georgian-inspired design adds to its ambiance, while comfort and facilities are average for a Broadway venue.
